==Problem==

What is the least possible value of
<cmath>(x+1)(x+2)(x+3)(x+4)+2019</cmath>where <imath>x</imath> is a real number?

<imath>\textbf{(A) } 2017 \qquad\textbf{(B) } 2018 \qquad\textbf{(C) } 2019 \qquad\textbf{(D) } 2020 \qquad\textbf{(E) } 2021</imath>

==Solution 1==
Grouping the first and last terms and two middle terms gives <imath>(x^2+5x+4)(x^2+5x+6)+2019</imath>, which can be simplified to <imath>(x^2+5x+5)^2-1+2019</imath>. Noting that squares are nonnegative, and verifying that <imath>x^2+5x+5=0</imath> for some real <imath>x</imath>, the answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(B) } 2018}</imath>.

==Solution 2 (Fakesolve)==

The largest number that makes this expression minimal is \( x = -1 \). This gives 2019, so is the answer 2019? Well, before we jump to conclusions, we need to understand that there may exist a number around or between the interval \( [-1, 0] \) such that this number \( n \) can make a smaller number. This interval is 1 unit long, so our answer is \( 2019 - 1 = \) <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(B) } 2018}</imath>.

~Pinotation

==Solution 3==
Let <imath>a=x+\tfrac{5}{2}</imath>. Then the expression <imath>(x+1)(x+2)(x+3)(x+4)</imath> becomes <imath>\left(a-\tfrac{3}{2}\right)\left(a-\tfrac{1}{2}\right)\left(a+\tfrac{1}{2}\right)\left(a+\tfrac{3}{2}\right)</imath>. 

We can now use the difference of two squares to get <imath>\left(a^2-\tfrac{9}{4}\right)\left(a^2-\tfrac{1}{4}\right)</imath>, and expand this to get <imath>a^4-\tfrac{5}{2}a^2+\tfrac{9}{16}</imath>.

Refactor this by completing the square to get <imath>\left(a^2-\tfrac{5}{4}\right)^2-1</imath>, which has a minimum value of <imath>-1</imath>. The answer is thus <imath>2019-1=\boxed{\textbf{(B) }2018}</imath>.

==Solution 4 (calculus)==

Similar to Solution 1, grouping the first and last terms and the middle terms, we get <imath>(x^2+5x+4)(x^2+5x+6)+2019</imath>. 

Letting <imath>y=x^2+5x</imath>, we get the expression <imath>(y+4)(y+6)+2019</imath>. Now, we can find the critical points of <imath>(y+4)(y+6)</imath> to minimize the function:

<imath>\frac{d}{dy}(y^2+10y+24)=0</imath>

<imath>2y+10=0</imath>

<imath>2y=-10</imath>

<imath>y=-5,0</imath>

To minimize the result, we use <imath>y=-5</imath>. Hence, the minimum is <imath>(-5+4)(-5+6)=-1</imath>, so <imath>-1+2019 = \boxed{\textbf{(B) }2018}</imath>.

''Note'': We could also have used the result that minimum/maximum point of a parabola <imath>y = ax^2 + bx + c</imath> occurs at <imath>x=-\frac{b}{2a}</imath>.

''Note 2:'' This solution is somewhat "lucky", since when we define variables to equal a function, and create another function out of these variables, the domain of such function may vary from the initial one. This is important because the maximum and minimum value of a function is dependent on its domain, e.g:

<imath>f(x)=x^2</imath> has no maximum value in the the integers, but once restricting the domain to <imath>(-5, 5)</imath> the maximum value of <imath>f(x)</imath> is <imath>25</imath>.

Also, observe that if we were to evaluate this by taking the derivative of <imath>(x+1)(x+2)(x+3)(x+4)+2019</imath>, we would get <imath>-5</imath> as the <imath>x</imath>-value to obtain the minimum <imath>y</imath>-value of this expression. It can be seen that <imath>-5</imath> is actually an inflection point, instead of a minimum or maximum. 

-Note 2 from Benedict T (countmath1)

==Solution 5(guess with answer choices)==

The expression is negative when an odd number of the factors are negative. This happens when <imath>-2 < x < -1</imath> or <imath>-4 < x < -3</imath>. Plugging in <imath>x = -\frac32</imath> or <imath>x = -\frac72</imath> yields <imath>-\frac{15}{16}</imath>, which is very close to <imath>-1</imath>. Thus the answer is <imath>-1 + 2019 = \boxed{\textbf{(B) }2018}</imath>.

==Solution 6 (using the answer choices) ==

Answer choices <imath>C</imath>, <imath>D</imath>, and <imath>E</imath> are impossible, since <imath>(x+1)(x+2)(x+3)(x+4)</imath> can be negative (as seen when e.g. <imath>x = -\frac{3}{2}</imath>). Plug in <imath>x = -\frac{3}{2}</imath> to see that it becomes <imath>2019 - \frac{15}{16}</imath>, so round this to <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(B) }2018}</imath>.

We can also see that the limit of the function is at least <imath>-1</imath> since at the minimum, two of the numbers are less than <imath>1</imath>, but two are between <imath>1</imath> and <imath>2</imath>.

==Solution 7 (also calculus but more convoluted)==
We can ignore the <imath>2019</imath> and consider it later, as it is a constant. By difference of squares, we can group this into <imath>\left((x+2.5)^2-0.5^2\right)\left((x+2.5)^2-1.5^2\right)</imath>. We pull a factor of <imath>4</imath> into each term to avoid dealing with decimals: 

<cmath>\dfrac{\left((2x+5)^2-1\right)\left((2x+5)^2-9\right)}{16}.</cmath>

Now, we let <imath>a=2x+5</imath>. Our expression becomes: 

<cmath>\dfrac{(a-1)(a-9)}{16}=\dfrac{a^2-10a+9}{16}.</cmath>

Taking the derivative, we get <imath>\dfrac{2a-10}{16}=\dfrac{a-5}8.</imath> This is equal to <imath>0</imath> when <imath>a=5</imath>, and plugging in <imath>a=5</imath>, we get the expression is equal to <imath>-1</imath> and therefore our answer is <imath>2019-1=\boxed{\text{(B)}~2018}.</imath>

~Technodoggo

==Solution 8 (basically a more detailed version of solution 1)==
<imath>(x+1)(x+2)(x+3)(x+4)</imath> can be rewritten as <imath>[(x+1)(x+4)][(x+2)(x+3)]=(x^2+5x+4)(x^2+5x+6)</imath>. Setting <imath>a=x^2+5x+5</imath> gives <imath>(a-1)(a+1)=a^2 -1</imath>. 

Then the whole problem can be written as the minimum value of <imath>(a^2 -1)+2019</imath>. <imath>\min(a^2)=0</imath> as long as <imath>x^2 +5x+5</imath> has at least one real root, which we can verify with <imath>(b^2-4ac) \to (5^2)-(4 \times 1 \times 5)=5 \geq 0</imath>. 
Thus, the answer is <imath>(0-1)+2019= \boxed{\textbf{(B) }2018}</imath>. 

~pandapower24
